judge_assessment.explanation: All three specific claims hold. Problem 2's stem reads "Find the missing angle B in this triangle. Then state whether the given data is AAS or ASA, and say how you can tell"; verify.json id 2 is a single triangle check solving for B with expected 65, so both the classification and its justification are unrecorded. The classification has a definite answer - the given side b = 12 lies between the given angles A = 35 and C = 80, which is ASA - so this is a checkable response left unchecked, not an inherently open one. Problem 6 asks the student to "name which angle you had to find first" (A = 71 degrees) alongside side b, and id 6 verifies only b = 9.77. Problem 8 says "Before computing, write down which angle is opposite the side you want - that is the pairing this problem is designed to test", and id 8 verifies only b = 81.14, so the sheet's own stated test object is the one thing not verified. And verify.json contains exactly one manual entry, on id 10. Every numeric answer recomputes as keyed: C = 75, B = 65, b = 18.03, a = 16.00, c = 14.25, b = 9.77, b = 93.47, b = 81.14, c = 82.61, a = 436.23. The judge's note that problem 10(b)'s AAS/ASA-versus-SSA explanation is honestly declared and mathematically sound also matches what I read.

strengths_to_preserve: Every figure is drawn to scale from its own givens and labels only that problem's data - I rendered page 5 and confirmed problem 8's triangle shows A = 63, B = 41, c = 120 with 'b = ?' on the side from A to C, which is correctly the side opposite B. No figure leaks values into a neighbouring problem.

The three traps are the three real Law-of-Sines errors and each is a computed number, not a label: 7.99 from flipping the ratio, 40.42 from inverting it, and 88.36 from using the wrong angle in the denominator. A grader seeing 88.36 on problem 8 knows precisely what happened.
Problems 7, 8 and 10 are genuine surveying, baseline and triangulation setups with metre units declared as answer_unit and printed as \answerline{m}, so the unit is bound data rather than decoration.

Problem 10(b) is the one item that genuinely cannot be computed - why AAS/ASA determines a unique triangle while SSA may not - and it is the one item declared manual, with a desc that states the target argument.

The study guide's Skill 1 gives the naming rule that problem 2 then tests ('AAS: the given side is opposite one of the given angles; ASA: the given side lies between the given angles') and its worked example names the case explicitly, so the classification skill is taught even though it is not verified.

root_causes.description: Coverage is per problem id, so problems 2, 6 and 8 - each of which prints a named classification or pairing alongside a computed value - satisfy the gate with the numeric check alone. The AAS/ASA classification and the opposite-angle pairing are both discrete, machine-checkable answers; nothing about them requires manual review, they simply have no representable type.
evidence: SKILL.md:189 - 'every problem id 1..N has at least one check'
verify.json id 2 is a lone triangle check solve_for B expected 65 while the stem also asks for the AAS/ASA classification
verify.json id 8 is a lone triangle check solve_for b while the stem asks which angle is opposite the side wanted
verify.py's triangle type accepts given/solve_for/expected only - there is no way to record 'the case is ASA' or 'the pairing is b with B'

root_causes.description: SKILL.md line 249 offers a reframing list (missing-number -> solve, ordering -> compare, and so on) but has no entry for 'classify this configuration' or 'name the matching pair', so an author facing a classification request has neither a type to use nor an instruction to declare it manual, and the request silently drops out of the manifest.

root_causes.description: The worksheet directions require side lengths rounded to two decimal places, but the Quick Answers bank prints problem 4 as '16.0' because _fmt echoes the JSON numeric verbatim and the JSON holds 16.0. The grader's scan column shows a different precision from the one the student was told to write.

improvements.title: Bind verification to every printed answer slot, not to one check per problem id
improvements.proposed_change: Count the responses each problem prints. Here problem 2 prints two (the angle and the AAS/ASA classification), problem 6 prints two (side b and the first-found angle A = 71), and problem 8 prints two (side b and the opposite-angle pairing). Pair this with a small extension to verify.py's triangle type - or a new 'choice' type with an allowed value set - so a classification like ASA becomes representable rather than merely required.
improvements.regression_test: Add a tests/fixtures case with a two-slot problem: the worksheet prints "(a) find the value ... (b) write the rule" under one \problem id while verify.json carries a single entry for that id. A new answer-slot gate must exit non-zero naming the id and the uncovered slot. Today build.sh exits 0 on exactly this shape, so the test fails before the fix and passes after.
improvements.expected_impact: The three flagged responses move inside the verification boundary. Because all three are discrete and checkable, this closes the hard failure without adding a single manual item.
improvements.risk: Slot counting from prose is heuristic; an over-eager counter could fail well-formed sheets. Mitigate by counting enumerated sub-parts and explicit "write ... on the answer line" phrases only, and by shipping the first release at exit 2 (manual review) rather than exit 1.

improvements.title: Require a manual entry whenever a problem asks the student to explain, name or justify
improvements.proposed_change: Extend SKILL.md's manual list to cover 'name the case and say how you can tell' style requests, and add the build lint so a stem containing an explain-class imperative without a manual entry fails. Problem 2's 'say how you can tell' is the justification half that stays open even once the ASA classification itself is machine-checked.
improvements.regression_test: Add tests/check_manual_coverage.py plus a fixture whose problem stem contains an explain-class imperative (explain / justify / name the error / say in words / state whether) while its verify.json id has no entry of type manual. The gate must exit non-zero. I ran this exact lint over the ten cases in this shard: it fires on curr-402 (7 ids), curr-406 (4), curr-419 (5), curr-426 (2), curr-438 (5) and curr-450 (3), and stays silent on all three ACCEPTs (curr-413, curr-425, curr-432) - zero false positives. Fails before the fix, passes after.
improvements.expected_impact: Problem 2 gains a manual entry for its justification while its classification is machine-verified - the correct seam, matching how problem 10 already splits a = 436.23 from the SSA discussion.
improvements.risk: Verb-list linting will miss paraphrases ("what does that tell you about ...") and could nag on stems that merely narrate. Keep the list short, allow an explicit per-problem opt-out field in the JSON, and ship at exit 2 first.

improvements.title: Print banked answers at the precision the worksheet demands
improvements.proposed_change: Let a verify entry declare the precision the stem requires (or infer it from an existing tol field) and have render_quick_answers format the banked value to that many decimal places, so a sheet that says 'round to two decimal places' banks 16.00 rather than 16.0. The docstring already promises verbatim Decimal echoing for exactly this reason; the gap is that the JSON literal itself was written short.
improvements.regression_test: Add a case to tests/test_render_quick_answers.py with expected 16.0 and a declared two-place precision, asserting the bank renders '16.00'. Fails today - _fmt returns repr/str of the literal.
improvements.expected_impact: Removes a small but visible inconsistency between the instruction the student reads and the answer the grader scans, on every sheet with a stated rounding rule.
improvements.risk: Over-formatting could pad exact integer answers with meaningless zeros; apply only where the entry or the sheet declares a rounding rule.

case_summary: Ten triangles, every one of them right - I recomputed all ten by hand (75, 65, 18.03, 16.00, 14.25, 9.77, 93.47, 81.14, 82.61, 436.23) and the figures render cleanly and to scale with correct opposite-side labelling. The failure is narrow and slightly ironic: problem 8's stem says the opposite-angle pairing 'is the pairing this problem is designed to test', and that pairing is the one response on the sheet with no verify entry. The same holds for problem 2's AAS/ASA classification and problem 6's first-found angle. None of the three is genuinely open - the classification is ASA, the pairing is b with B, the first angle is 71 degrees - they are simply not representable in any verify type, and the per-id coverage rule lets the numeric check stand in for them. Problem 10 shows the author knew where the real manual seam was and put it in the right place. A smaller issue the judge did not note: the bank prints 16.0 where the directions demand two decimal places.
